title: Tools at hand
hook: Marcus Aurelius, in army camps on the frontier, tells himself to keep his principles ready like a physician's instruments
tomorrow: Zoe won't ask anyone for help. what did Ayyub do at the bottom?

segments.voice: This week's lines come back in the games: a share, peacemaker, speak up, quiet good, in the world, one arrow. Yesterday's was one arrow: the first one hurts; the second can fly past. Today, what to reach for when it hits.
screen: `SIX LINES COME BACK.` → `ONE ARROW.` → `NOW, WHAT TO REACH FOR.`

segments.voice: A first-aid kit under the sink. A spare key with a neighbor. A number saved for emergencies. Ready before it's needed. Marcus Aurelius was emperor of Rome, and he kept a notebook written to himself. One section ends with a line saying it was written among the Quadi, far from Rome. Tradition places those notes in his army camps on the frontier. And in them, he reaches for a picture of tools.
screen: `A KIT UNDER THE SINK.` → `AN EMPEROR IN AN ARMY CAMP.` → `NOTES TO HIMSELF.` → `AMONG THE QUADI.`

segments.voice: Here's his picture, from the third book of the Meditations: physicians always keep their instruments and knives at hand for sudden cases. So keep your principles ready, he tells himself, for understanding things divine and human. And from the fourth book: people seek retreats in the country, at the seashore, in the hills. But you can retire into yourself at any hour. So keep a few brief, basic principles there, ready to hand. That's the Stoic teaching: a small set of true principles, rehearsed in calm, so that when the blow lands you don't have to invent wisdom on the spot. Practiced in the quiet, used in the storm. And this week you've been filling a kit. One arrow, not two. Speak up when it's clear. Quiet good. A share. Tools like these don't help in a drawer. They help ready to hand.
screen: `THE PHYSICIAN'S INSTRUMENTS.` · `A RETREAT INTO YOURSELF.` · `REHEARSED IN CALM.` · `A KIT FROM THIS WEEK.` · then, large: `TOOLS READY.`

segments.voice: Name your three best tools for a hard day: a line you trust, a person you can call, a practice that steadies you. Count them on three fingers. Then rest your hand and breathe, like a doctor checking the kit before a shift.
Tools at hand: the Stoic habit of keeping a few true principles ready, like a physician's instruments, for the moment trouble comes.
Your line: tools ready. Marcus kept his principles the way a physician keeps his knives. That's the week, day 1736.

howItsDone: Readers of the Stoics keep short principles ready, often written out or memorized, and review them in the morning or evening so they come to mind under stress. Marcus Aurelius's Meditations is itself a notebook of such reminders.
